teaser: A princess locked in a tower, a god disguised as rain, and one small black rectangle.
review_notes:
Klimt bought back the University ceiling paintings in 1905 (with help from patrons) after years of controversy.
Danaë is dated 1907 (often 1907-08) and was reportedly shown at the 1908 Kunstschau in Vienna.
The black rectangle among the gold is commonly read as a male symbol: an interpretation, presented as such.
Size approx. 77 x 83 cm.
Klimt's father Ernst was a gold engraver.

lesson.text: It starts with a refusal. Around 1900 the Austrian state had ordered three huge ceiling paintings from Klimt for the University of Vienna. Professors signed a petition against them. Critics called them ugly and indecent. In 1905 Klimt gave up, paid the money back and took his canvases home.

From then on he avoided public commissions and painted what he liked for private buyers. Two years later he chose a Greek myth that Titian and Rembrandt had painted before him, and treated it with a frankness no ministry would have accepted.

The story: a king hears a prophecy that his grandson will kill him. So he locks his only daughter, Danaë, in a sealed room where no man can reach her. Zeus, king of the gods, gets in anyway, by turning himself into a shower of gold.
In the myth, the father's plan fails completely. Danaë gives birth to the hero Perseus, who years later throws a discus at an athletic contest and kills his grandfather by accident.
Older painters showed a bedroom: a bed, curtains, often a servant trying to catch the falling coins. Klimt throws all of that out. See what is left once the furniture is gone.
Two movements fill this small, nearly square canvas.

lines.label: The curl
lines.text: Head, hair, veil, hip and raised thigh form one closed loop. Danaë is curled up like a sleeper, or like a child before birth. The loop touches every edge of the frame.

lines.label: The rain
lines.text: The gold enters at the top left and pours down behind her thigh in a single stream. It is the only thing in the picture that comes from outside.

lines.label: Skin against dark
lines.text: A diagonal cuts the picture in two halves: pale flesh above, a dark transparent veil below. There is no floor, no wall, no horizon to tell you where she is.

lesson.text: The body is pushed so close that one thigh takes up almost a third of the canvas. You are not looking into a room. You are inside the tower with her, far closer than a polite viewer would stand.
Klimt tells the myth without any setting. The body itself becomes the whole composition, folded to fit a nearly square frame.
Now the gold. It is painted as coins, flecks and bright scribbles. Among all those round shapes, Klimt slipped in one that is not round at all.
Somewhere in the stream of gold there is a single black, upright rectangle. Tap it.

spots.title: The intruder
spots.text: A small black bar outlined in gold stands among the coins on the left edge. Klimt often used hard rectangles as a male sign and circles as a female one. Many read this as Zeus himself.

lesson.text: Once you know that code, the veil on the right reads differently too. It is scattered with gold rings and rounded shapes: the feminine side of the picture, facing the single hard rectangle across the body.

Gold was a family matter. Klimt's father was a gold engraver, and Gustav grew up watching the metal being worked. As a painter he used real gold leaf, thin sheets of beaten gold, glued onto the canvas.
And Danaë herself? In older versions she looks up at the rain, surprised or welcoming. Klimt's Danaë looks at nothing.

lesson.title: What she feels
lesson.text: Two details carry the emotion of the picture.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Eyes closed, lips parted, cheeks flushed pink. She is asleep or lost in sensation. This expression of open pleasure is what made the painting daring in 1907.

spots.title: The hand
spots.text: Her fingers curl tightly into the patterned cloth by her chest. It is a tense gesture in a body that otherwise looks completely relaxed.

spots.title: The red hair
spots.text: A mass of red-orange waves fills the top right corner. Klimt gave this fiery hair to many of his women. Here it works like a second blanket around her head.

lesson.text: Vienna in those years was the city of Sigmund Freud, where doctors and writers were starting to talk openly about dreams and desire. Klimt paints the same subject, with a myth as his excuse.

The canvas is only about 77 by 83 centimeters (roughly 30 by 33 inches), smaller than many posters of it. It belongs to a private collection in Vienna, so it is seen in public far less often than The Kiss.

The officials who rejected Klimt in 1905 wanted him to decorate a ceiling with something noble. He answered with a sleeping woman, a handful of gold and one black rectangle. Which of the two do you think people would still be looking at today?

quiz.question: Why did Danaë's father lock her away?
options: A prophecy said her son would kill him
quiz.explanation: He feared the prophecy that his grandson would kill him.

quiz.question: In what form does Zeus reach Danaë?
quiz.explanation: Zeus turns himself into golden rain to enter the sealed room.

quiz.question: What did Klimt remove compared with older paintings of this myth?
options: The bedroom, the bed and the servant
quiz.explanation: He drops the whole setting and keeps only the body, the veil and the gold.

quiz.question: What is the small black rectangle among the gold often read as?
options: A male symbol standing for Zeus
quiz.explanation: Klimt used hard rectangles as a male sign, and many see Zeus in it.

quiz.question: What had happened to Klimt two years before he painted Danaë?
options: He gave up a state commission after his university paintings were attacked
He won a gold medal in Paris
quiz.explanation: In 1905 he repaid the state and took back his rejected ceiling paintings.

facts.text: Klimt's Danaë looks up in surprise at the falling gold.
facts.explanation: Her eyes are closed and she looks at nothing.

facts.text: Klimt's father worked with gold as an engraver.
facts.explanation: Gustav grew up around the metal, which he later used as real gold leaf.

facts.text: The painting shows the tower room in detail, with a bed and curtains.
facts.explanation: Klimt removed every piece of setting, so only body, veil and gold remain.
